title_en: The Ruling on Voluntary Prayers for One Who Has Prayers to Make Up
body_ar:
ما حكم التنفل لمن عليه قضاء الصلاة من زمن الشباب؟

أن الإنسان إذا كان فرط في صلاة بعينها وهو يعلمها أو في صلوات فعليه أن يقضي تلك الصلوات أما إذا كان مقصرا فقط كأن يصليها بتيمم وهو قادر على الوضوء أو الغسل أو نحو ذلك فلا قضاء عليه لتلك الصلوات ويكمل النقص الحاصل بالنوافل فالنوافل مكملة للفرائض وهي تكملها يوم القيامة، فإن الله تعالى يقول لملائكته عندما يبدأ حساب عبد من عباده انظروا هل لعبدي من نفل فيتمم له فرضه.
body_en:
What is the ruling on performing voluntary prayers for one who has prayers to make up from the time of his youth?

If a person omitted a particular prayer that he knows of, or a number of prayers, then he must make up those prayers. But if he was merely deficient — as, for instance, that he prayed them with dry ablution (tayammum) while able to perform ablution or the full washing, or the like — then there is no making up (qaḍāʾ) upon him for those prayers, and he makes good the shortfall that has occurred by means of the voluntary prayers. For the voluntary acts complete the obligatory ones, and they will complete them on the Day of Resurrection: God, exalted, says to His angels when the reckoning of one of His servants begins, 'Look — has My servant any voluntary prayer?' — and it is used to complete his obligatory prayer for him.

flags.arabic: ما حكم التنفل لمن عليه قضاء الصلاة
flags.context: the question asked, set against the answer given
options: render both faithfully and mark that the question asked is not the question answered
present the answer as permitting voluntary prayers while make-ups are outstanding
present the answer as requiring make-ups before voluntary prayers
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY — TITLE/QUESTION AND BODY DO NOT MEET. The question, and the title, ask whether a person with outstanding missed prayers may perform VOLUNTARY prayers — a real and disputed question, on which some jurists hold that make-ups take precedence. The Sheikh does not answer it. He answers a different question: which past prayers must be made up at all, distinguishing outright omission from deficient performance. He then says the deficient ones are made good by voluntary prayers, which touches the questioner's concern only obliquely. A reader will take the answer for a permission, and the site must not present it as one. Nothing has been supplied in either direction.

flags.context: the distinction on which the whole answer turns
flags.note: These two words carry the entire ruling, and blurring them would make the answer incoherent. farraṭa is failing to perform the prayer at all; muqaṣṣir is performing it but defectively, and the Sheikh's own example — praying with tayammum while able to use water — makes the sense unmistakable. The consequence differs absolutely: the first requires qaḍāʾ, the second does not. The English keeps them lexically distinct throughout.

flags.arabic: انظروا هل لعبدي من نفل فيتمم له فرضه
flags.context: the report quoted as evidence, introduced as God's speech to the angels
options: render in quotation marks as reported divine speech, not in Qur'anic braces
render in the curly braces used for Qur'anic quotation
flags.note: The Sheikh introduces this with 'God, exalted, says to His angels', but it is not Qur'an: it is a prophetic report, given here in a compressed paraphrase rather than in the wording of any collection. House style reserves curly braces for Qur'an, so ordinary quotation marks have been used. He names no narrator, no collection and no grading, and none has been supplied.
